summary: Gives examples of how iSCSI names are built and discusses how initiators find iSCSI targets. It aims for flexibility, serving both small isolated setups and large environments that need secure, scalable discovery. It complements the main iSCSI document and was updated by RFC 7143.

plainLanguage.summary: iSCSI systems need a stable name for each initiator or storage target and an address for reaching it. RFC 3721 explains two name formats, optional display aliases, and several ways an initiator can discover targets.

subtitle: How iSCSI nodes are named, how initiators find targets, and what aliases are for.

tldr.problem: iSCSI initiators need stable names for targets and a way to discover an address where each target can be reached.
tldr.mechanism: The memo explains the iqn. and eui. name formats, optional human-readable aliases, and static, SendTargets, and zero-configuration discovery.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3721 is an Informational companion to RFC 3720 and has been updated by RFC 7143. It also discusses proxies, firewalls, and the relationship between node names and security identifiers.

today: RFC 3721 is an Informational document that has been updated by RFC 7143. It complements the iSCSI protocol specification, RFC 3720.

sections.title: The Difference Between a Name and an Address
sections.content:
An iSCSI node can be an initiator, a target, or both. Its iSCSI name is a permanent, location-independent identifier used for management and as a principal object in authentication. The name belongs to the node, not its network adapter, so the node can move between hosts without losing associated SCSI state.

An iSCSI address combines the node name with a TCP location: a domain name or IP address and, for a target, an optional port. If the target port is absent, the default is 3260. A node may have multiple addresses, and those addresses can change while the name remains the same.
sections.plainLanguage: An iSCSI name identifies a node, while an address tells an initiator where to contact it. The address can change without changing the node's name.

sections.title: The iqn. and eui. Name Formats
sections.content:
An iqn. name contains the prefix, a year-and-month code, a reversed domain name that identifies the naming authority, and optionally a colon followed by a string chosen by that authority. The authority is responsible for making the complete names it assigns unique. The domain component identifies who assigns the name; it does not identify where the node is located.

An eui. name contains an IEEE EUI-64 identifier written in ASCII hexadecimal. These two formats give naming authorities different ways to create unique node names.
sections.plainLanguage: An iqn. name records the naming authority and a string that authority assigns. An eui. name uses an IEEE identifier; neither format gives the node's network location.

sections.title: Aliases Are for Display Only
sections.content:
An alias is an optional UTF-8 text description for an initiator or target. It can help a person recognize a device in a management display, but it does not have to be unique and must not be used to identify, address, or authenticate a node.

The alias is exchanged at login and may be ignored by a device that does not display it. The RFC defines it as a variable-length string of 0 to 255 characters, terminated by at least one NULL character.
sections.plainLanguage: An alias is a readable label that helps people recognize a device. The protocol must use the iSCSI name, not the alias, to identify or authenticate the node.

sections.title: Three Ways to Discover Targets
sections.content:
Before opening an iSCSI session, an initiator needs the target's IP address, TCP port, and iSCSI name. Static configuration supplies all three in advance and requires no discovery. SendTargets assumes the initiator already knows the network entity's address and port, then lets it ask which targets are available there.

Zero-configuration discovery assumes the initiator knows nothing about the target. It can multicast discovery messages or contact storage name servers. The memo identifies SLP as able to provide the needed discovery functions and iSNS as an option for added management functions, including notification and access management.
sections.plainLanguage: An initiator can use a preconfigured list, ask a known network entity for its targets, or start discovery without knowing a target in advance. The method depends on what information the initiator already has.

sections.title: Intermediaries and Security Identity
sections.content:
The appendices describe how iSCSI can work through port redirectors, SOCKS servers, SCSI gateways, iSCSI proxies, and stateful inspection firewalls. Because a redirector can change IP or TCP header information, iSCSI data integrity checks must not include those headers. An iSCSI proxy that terminates the protocol on both sides needs separate checks for headers and data so data integrity can be checked end to end through the proxy.

In an untrusted environment, a node name alone may not prove who is requesting access. The target can use a separate security identifier and authentication method, then check that the authenticated identity is authorized to use the claimed InitiatorName.
sections.plainLanguage: A proxy or redirector can change network details while forwarding iSCSI traffic. In untrusted settings, the target must also check that an authenticated user is allowed to use the initiator name presented at login.
